canonical_policy.name: Application Services are default orchestration
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: Use Application Services as the default orchestration mechanism for use cases.

reviews.boundary_analysis: Large-service size alone is not a pattern-adoption justification; infrastructure hooks cannot hide business behavior. Both elaborations beyond default orchestration already registered.

context_quotes:
- Default: Application Services orchestrate use cases, coordinating Domain objects, repositories, external-service abstractions, and the Unit of Work. A service growing too large is a signal to reconsider its responsibilities, not an automatic reason for another pattern.
- Application must define the persistence and external-service abstractions its use cases require and keep infrastructure implementation details out.

- [ ] Role and dependency rules — `.claude/rules/backend/architecture-style.md` and `.claude/rules/backend/architecture.md` (thin controllers, Application Services orchestrate, inward references, commit boundary).
- [ ] Repository contracts and persistence boundary — `.claude/rules/backend/persistence.md`, `.claude/rules/backend/persistence-technology.md`.
Use interceptors for infrastructure-level cross-cutting behavior with a clear benefit, such as auditing; never hide business behavior in them.
Use a `DelegatingHandler` for genuine HTTP pipeline concerns — authorization header acquisition, correlation/context propagation, request signing — never for business decisions.

canonical_policy.name: Application owns use-case abstractions
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: Define persistence and external-service abstractions in Application when use cases require them; keep infrastructure implementation details out.

reviews.boundary_analysis: Caller-identity abstraction is conditional on repeated need, with explicit-id simplification; scopes resolve orchestration rather than Infrastructure internals. Existing records preserve these qualifications; boundary abstraction vs concrete helper is already uncertain in independent.

context_quotes:
- Default: Application Services orchestrate use cases, coordinating Domain objects, repositories, external-service abstractions, and the Unit of Work. A service growing too large is a signal to reconsider its responsibilities, not an automatic reason for another pattern.
- Application must define the persistence and external-service abstractions its use cases require and keep infrastructure implementation details out.
- Application must not depend on persistence-technology types or APIs (database context, entity sets, query or provider types) or on ASP.NET Core transport types.

- Default: specific repository interfaces that represent actual, cohesive Application persistence needs, not table-mirroring generic CRUD contracts. Repository interfaces are defined in Application and implemented in Infrastructure.
- Repository interfaces must not expose `IQueryable<T>`, database-context or entity-set types, query expressions, or provider-specific types; query construction stays in Infrastructure. Return materialized entities, collections, projections, or explicit result models.

When use cases repeatedly need caller identity, define a small Application abstraction and implement the HTTP adapter at an outer boundary; Application services never depend on `HttpContext`, `ClaimsPrincipal`, or `IHttpContextAccessor`. Skip `ICurrentUser` when passing an explicit user identifier is simpler.

Hardcoded signing keys, authorization only in the frontend, Application depending on `HttpContext`, 401 for authenticated-but-forbidden or 403 for missing authentication, role/permission magic strings throughout the codebase, adding Identity, JWT issuance, or OIDC infrastructure without an actual need.

Use abstractions at architectural boundaries (Application services, repositories, external adapters); concrete registration is fine for implementation-only helpers without a separate contract.

Never register an Application service that depends on scoped repositories as a singleton. A singleton or hosted service that needs scoped work creates a scope per operation and resolves a scoped orchestration service, not Infrastructure internals:

Application defines the persistence contracts (specific repository interfaces and `IUnitOfWork`); Infrastructure implements them with EF Core. `DbContext` already provides change tracking and unit-of-work behavior internally; `IUnitOfWork` is the Application-facing abstraction over that commit boundary, and its implementation delegates to the same scoped `DbContext`.

| Scenario | Default technique |
|---|---|
| Application persistence dependency | Specific repository interface |
| Commit application changes | `IUnitOfWork.SaveChangesAsync` |
| Read-only entity query | `AsNoTracking()` when useful |
| Read model | Database-side projection |
| Primary-key entity lookup | `FindAsync` when its semantics fit |
| Complex entity graph | Explicit `Include` / projection |
| Set-based mass update/delete | `ExecuteUpdateAsync` / `ExecuteDeleteAsync` when appropriate |
| Measured extremely hot query | Consider a compiled query |
| Multiple commits requiring atomicity | Explicit transaction (inside the execution strategy) |
| Production schema change | Reviewed migration, scripted deployment |
| Fresh local seed dataset | Developer drops and recreates the local database |
Application may define an abstraction; Infrastructure implements it with `HttpClient`, so Application does not know the service uses HTTP:

```text
backend/ProjectName.Application/
├── Abstractions/
│   ├── Persistence/          # IOrderRepository.cs, IUnitOfWork.cs — no persistence-technology types
│   └── ExternalServices/     # IEmailSender.cs, ICurrentUser.cs ... — only once such dependencies exist
├── Services/                 # IOrderService.cs, OrderService.cs (Application Services)
├── DTOs/                     # Application operation/data models when useful; not a dumping ground
├── Validation/               # FluentValidation validators for Application input/use-case rules
└── DependencyInjection.cs    # AddApplication(): Application services and validation only
```

```text
backend/ProjectName.Infrastructure/
├── Persistence/              # persistence implementation; internal layout: persistence-change
├── Services/                 # EmailSender.cs, FileStorage.cs ... implementations of Application abstractions
└── DependencyInjection.cs    # AddInfrastructure(configuration): persistence, repositories, IUnitOfWork, adapters, HttpClient integrations, resilience handlers when used
```

canonical_policy.name: No infrastructure/transport types in Application
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: Application must not depend on DbContext, DbSet, EF Core APIs/provider types, or ASP.NET Core transport types.

reviews.boundary_analysis: Technology-neutral wording broadens EF-specific canonical examples, explicit ClaimsPrincipal exclusion and package-wide detector scope already recorded. Repository query-expression ban considered under ARC014.

context_quotes:
- Dependencies must point inward: Domain references no other application project; Application references Domain; Infrastructure references Application and Domain; Api references Application and may reference Infrastructure only for composition and dependency registration. Inner layers never depend on outer layers, and Domain and Application never reference Infrastructure-specific types.
- If a feature seems to need an outward reference, reconsider the abstraction boundary instead of adding the reference.

- Application must define the persistence and external-service abstractions its use cases require and keep infrastructure implementation details out.
- Application must not depend on persistence-technology types or APIs (database context, entity sets, query or provider types) or on ASP.NET Core transport types.
Binds to the architecture frame: EF Core lives in the Infrastructure role and implements the Application persistence and commit-boundary contracts.

- EF Core is an Infrastructure implementation detail. Use its full capabilities inside Infrastructure, but EF Core concepts — `DbContext`, `DbSet<T>`, EF Core APIs, `IQueryable<T>` backed by EF Core, and provider-specific types — must not leak into Application.
- Infrastructure implements `IUnitOfWork` by delegating to the shared scoped `AppDbContext`.

Authentication/authorization middleware normally produces these responses rather than controllers manufacturing them.

## Current user

Controllers may read `User` for purely HTTP-specific information:

```csharp
[Authorize]
[HttpGet("me")]
public ActionResult<CurrentUserResponse> GetCurrentUser() =>
    Ok(new CurrentUserResponse(User.FindFirstValue(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier)));
```

When use cases repeatedly need caller identity, define a small Application abstraction and implement the HTTP adapter at an outer boundary; Application services never depend on `HttpContext`, `ClaimsPrincipal`, or `IHttpContextAccessor`. Skip `ICurrentUser` when passing an explicit user identifier is simpler.

```csharp
public interface ICurrentUser
{
    string? UserId { get; }
    bool IsAuthenticated { get; }
}
```

## Cookies, CSRF, and token storage

CSRF and token-storage rules: `.claude/rules/frontend/security.md`. Technique for cookie authentication: ASP.NET Core antiforgery (`AddAntiforgery`, token validation on state-changing endpoints) paired with the SPA's matching XSRF header handling. Signing secrets follow the configuration and secret rules.

Hardcoded signing keys, authorization only in the frontend, Application depending on `HttpContext`, 401 for authenticated-but-forbidden or 403 for missing authentication, role/permission magic strings throughout the codebase, adding Identity, JWT issuance, or OIDC infrastructure without an actual need.

Never solve an architectural dependency problem with an invalid project reference (e.g. Application → Infrastructure to make a type compile). Invalid shortcuts also include leaking persistence-technology types into Application, moving business logic into controllers, replacing server authorization with frontend-only guards, and scattering HTTP calls into components to bypass a data-access service. Read `.claude/rules/backend/architecture-style.md` for backend repairs and `.claude/rules/frontend/` for frontend repairs. Frontend shortcuts to refuse: converting code to `any` to silence the compiler, disabling strict mode, suppressing template diagnostics without understanding them, replacing framework APIs speculatively, adding another state-management or HTTP library to bypass a local issue.

- [ ] Role and dependency rules — `.claude/rules/backend/architecture-style.md` and `.claude/rules/backend/architecture.md` (thin controllers, Application Services orchestrate, inward references, commit boundary).
- [ ] Repository contracts and persistence boundary — `.claude/rules/backend/persistence.md`, `.claude/rules/backend/persistence-technology.md`.
- [ ] Proportionality — consequential patterns or extra abstractions appear only with an approved need (`CLAUDE.md`, Decision control).

```text
backend/ProjectName.Application/
├── Abstractions/
│   ├── Persistence/          # IOrderRepository.cs, IUnitOfWork.cs — no persistence-technology types
│   └── ExternalServices/     # IEmailSender.cs, ICurrentUser.cs ... — only once such dependencies exist
├── Services/                 # IOrderService.cs, OrderService.cs (Application Services)
├── DTOs/                     # Application operation/data models when useful; not a dumping ground
├── Validation/               # FluentValidation validators for Application input/use-case rules
└── DependencyInjection.cs    # AddApplication(): Application services and validation only
```

```text
ProjectName.Domain          -> (no application project references)
ProjectName.Application     -> ProjectName.Domain
ProjectName.Infrastructure  -> ProjectName.Application, ProjectName.Domain
ProjectName.Api             -> ProjectName.Application, ProjectName.Infrastructure
```

canonical_policy.name: No CQRS/mediator/VSA by default
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: Do not introduce CQRS handlers, MediatR, Kommand, Vertical Slice Architecture or similar mediator-based organization unless explicitly approved.

reviews.boundary_analysis: Explicit approval gate remains; review cannot demand unadopted patterns. Broader named nondefault patterns have explicit existing coverage, not novel synonyms.

context_quotes: Do not introduce or enforce patterns the repository has not adopted (see the decision register's not-adopted styles); differing from an unadopted pattern is not a finding.

MediatR, CQRS handler trees, Vertical Slice Architecture, Domain Events, Specifications, SharedKernel, BuildingBlocks, EventBus, messaging, microservices, Kubernetes, cloud-specific projects, state-management frameworks — each requires an approved need (decision register; `CLAUDE.md`, Decision control).

|---|---|---|---|
| architecture (required frame) | clean-architecture | — | Backend roles Domain, Application, Infrastructure, Api as `backend/<Name>.<Layer>/`; role rules in the architecture-style standard (loads with backend files). Not adopted: CQRS handlers, MediatR, Kommand, Vertical Slice Architecture, or similar mediator-based organization; introducing any of them requires explicit approval. |
| persistence (required leaf) | ef-core, provider variant sqlserver | `ef-core` | Default persistence: EF Core with Microsoft SQL Server (`Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.SqlServer`); provider-specific concerns stay out of Application and Domain. Migration mechanism: EF Core migrations. Seeding mechanism: dedicated Development seeder. String comparison follows database collation (SQL Server default collations are case-insensitive); observable semantics remain a product decision. Binds: architecture. |

canonical_policy.name: Controllers are thin HTTP entry points
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: ASP.NET Core Controllers are the default HTTP entry point; they bind/validate input, invoke Application services, and translate outcomes to HTTP responses.

reviews.boundary_analysis: Default Controllers becomes explicit-request gate for Minimal API groups; related version/filter examples and metadata-based output caching have narrower procedural guidance. Existing records cover each, so no new unconditional ban inferred.

context_quotes:
- ASP.NET Core Controllers are the default HTTP entry point and must stay thin: bind and validate HTTP input, invoke Application services, and translate Application outcomes into HTTP responses.
- Controllers must not contain business logic, access the database context or concrete repositories, or construct infrastructure services manually.
Minimal API version-group examples in a Controller-based project, a new version for every implementation change, silently removing deprecated versions.

Returning raw exception messages, inconsistent anonymous error objects, putting business rules only in request validators, and coupling validation to Minimal API endpoint filters when Controllers are the HTTP model.
Apply the policy through controller/action metadata. Never cache authenticated or user-specific responses unless the key and policy isolate users and authorization context.

- [ ] Role and dependency rules — `.claude/rules/backend/architecture-style.md` and `.claude/rules/backend/architecture.md` (thin controllers, Application Services orchestrate, inward references, commit boundary).
- [ ] Repository contracts and persistence boundary — `.claude/rules/backend/persistence.md`, `.claude/rules/backend/persistence-technology.md`.
Application expresses meaningful outcomes without `IActionResult`, `ProblemDetails`, or status codes; the controller maps them.

├── Middleware/               # only when custom middleware exists
├── Extensions/               # cohesive composition extensions; do not move code just to shorten Program.cs
├── Program.cs                # composition root: AddApplication(); AddInfrastructure(builder.Configuration)
├── appsettings.json
└── appsettings.Development.json
```

Controllers are the HTTP endpoint mechanism; create Minimal API endpoint groups only when explicitly requested. Api references Infrastructure only for composition — controllers never consume Infrastructure implementation types directly. Use `Contracts/` for transport-specific contracts only when separation from Application models provides value.
